Cascading

/kas-KAY-ding/ - the stress falls on KAY · adjective

Hear It

No recording available for this word.

What It Means

Cascading means passing along in a chain, with each stage setting off the next.

One rumor about the bank's losses set off a cascading run of withdrawals that spread to three neighboring lenders by Friday.

Worked Example

When otters vanished from the kelp coast, the effects were cascading: urchins the otters had eaten multiplied unchecked, the urchins mowed down the kelp, and the fish that sheltered in the kelp disappeared with it.

Cascading is the word for trouble that travels — each failure is the direct cause of the next, like water spilling down a staircase of rock. A string of unrelated mishaps is not cascading; the chain is the point.

How Cascading Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

snowballing

snowballing: growing bigger as it rolls, with size rather than sequence in view

chain-reaction

chain-reaction: used as a label for the linked process itself, especially in physics

rippling

rippling: spreading outward in gentle waves, without cascade's sense of gathering force

Antonyms

contained

contained: held within limits so it cannot spread

self-limiting

self-limiting: burning itself out instead of feeding the next stage

How Strong Is It? — rippling → cascading → runaway

rippling vs. cascading

rippling vs. cascading: Rippling is milder than cascading — ripples spread and fade, while a cascading failure gathers force with each stage it topples.

runaway vs. cascading

runaway vs. cascading: Runaway is stronger than cascading — a cascading failure still moves stage by stage, but a runaway one has stopped answering to any brake at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cascad-

Root — cascad-: waterfall (Italian cascata, 'a fall', from Latin cadere)

Suffix — -ing

Suffix — -ing: adjective: doing the action

Put it together

Put it together: Cascad- (from Italian cascata, a waterfall, built on Latin cadere, 'to fall') + -ing = falling like a waterfall. A cascade drops from ledge to ledge, each pool spilling into the next — exactly the picture the word paints when failures, delays, or losses pour from one stage down into the one below.

Word Choice

neutral / technical

Cascading is the engineer's and economist's word for linked failure — grids, markets, schedules, and ecosystems all suffer cascading effects. Use it only when each stage genuinely causes the next; for trouble that merely grows bigger as it goes, snowballing is the better fit.
